t: Rohit said, "I had completed the project."
o: Rohit said he has completed the project.
Rohit said he completed the project.
Rohit said that he had completed the project.
Rohit said that he was completing the project.
e: This tests an important exception to the backshift rule: Past Perfect is already the 'furthest back' past tense in English, so it has nowhere further to shift — it simply stays as 'had completed'. Many students assume every tense must change and wrongly pick option (a) or (b), but reducing Past Perfect to Present Perfect or Simple Past would actually distort the timeline and change the meaning. Option (d) is wrong because it turns a completed action into an ongoing one. Remember: once a sentence is already in Past Perfect, indirect speech leaves it exactly as it is.

t: The geologist explained that tectonic shifts were inevitable.
o: The geologist said, "Tectonic shifts are inevitable."
"Tectonic shifts were inevitable," said the geologist.
The geologist explained, "Tectonic shifts will occur."
"Inevitably, tectonic shifts occur," he said.
e: This is another Universal Truth question, presented in reverse (Indirect to Direct) and worded as a general scientific statement, which is treated as a timeless fact. Even though the indirect version uses the past tense 'were' (because 'explained' is a past reporting verb), the correct Direct Speech restores the Present Tense — 'are inevitable' — since universal or general truths keep the present tense in their original quoted form. Option (b) wrongly keeps 'were' straight from the indirect sentence, option (c) changes the meaning into a future prediction, and option (d) rewords the sentence instead of accurately reconstructing what was actually said.

t: The scientist stated that water boiled at 100 degrees Celsius.
o: "Water will boil at 100 degrees Celsius," said the scientist.
"Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius," the scientist stated.
"Water had boiled at 100 degrees Celsius," said the scientist.
"Water is boiling at 100 degrees Celsius," said the scientist.
e: Scientific facts are Universal Truths, so regardless of the past tense 'boiled' appearing in the indirect sentence, the original Direct Speech must be restored to the Simple Present Tense — 'boils' — because this is a permanent property of water, not a one-time past event. Option (a) wrongly turns it into a future prediction, option (c) makes it sound like a completed past event rather than a fact, and option (d) incorrectly uses Present Continuous, as if the boiling were happening right now instead of describing a general truth.

t: Mrs. Gomes said, "Virtue is its own reward."
o: Mrs. Gomes said that Virtue was its own reward.
Mrs. Gomes said that Virtue is its own reward.
Mrs. Gomes said that Virtue had its own reward.
Mrs. Gomes said that Virtue has its own reward.
e: 'Virtue is its own reward' is a well-known moral proverb, and like scientific facts, proverbs and universally accepted truths keep their Present Tense in indirect speech even after a past reporting verb. Option (a) incorrectly backshifts to the past tense, option (c) changes the meaning entirely (as if virtue 'possessed' a reward in the past), and option (d) wrongly uses Present Perfect. The safe rule: any timeless statement of wisdom or morality is exempt from backshifting.

t: Mona said to me, "Are you planning a trip to Disneyland?"
o: Mona enquired of me if I was planning a trip to Disneyland.
Mona asked me that was I planning a trip to Disneyland?
Mona enquired of me that was I planning a trip to Disneyland.
Mona asked me if I had been planning a trip to Disneyland?
e: This is another Yes/No question, so it must be converted using 'if' or 'whether' with no inversion. The correct pattern is 'enquired of me if I was planning...' — subject 'I' comes before the verb 'was', exactly like a normal statement. Options (b) and (c) both incorrectly keep the inverted question form 'was I' and also wrongly mix 'that' with a question — 'that' should never introduce a Yes/No question; only 'if' or 'whether' can. Option (d) wrongly over-backshifts Present Continuous all the way to Past Perfect Continuous, when it should only move one step to Past Continuous.

t: She said, "Why didn't you tell me the truth earlier?"
o: She asked why I hadn't told her the truth earlier.
She asked why hadn't I told her the truth earlier.
She said why I didn't tell her the truth earlier.
She questioned why did I not tell her the truth.
e: Negative Simple Past 'didn't tell' backshifts to negative Past Perfect 'hadn't told', following the same logic as positive sentences. As always with Wh-questions, statement word order is required — 'why I hadn't told her', not 'why hadn't I told her', which wrongly keeps the inverted question form. Option (b) makes exactly this inversion error. Option (c) uses correct word order but fails to backshift the tense at all. Option (d) both keeps the inverted 'did I not' structure and drops the required time phrase 'earlier'.

t: The boss said to the secretary, "Don't forget to order A3 size paper."
o: The boss instructed the secretary not to forget to order A3 size paper.
The boss told the secretary that she didn't forget to order A3 size paper.
The boss asked the secretary to order A3 size paper.
The boss told the secretary that she should not forget to order A3 size paper.
e: Negative Imperatives ('Don't...') are converted using the pattern: reporting verb plus object plus 'not to' plus base verb. Here, 'Don't forget' correctly becomes 'not to forget', with 'instructed' as an appropriate reporting verb for a boss giving a directive to a secretary. Option (b) incorrectly uses a 'that'-clause with simple past tense, losing the instructional force of the original. Option (c) oversimplifies the meaning by dropping 'Don't forget' and just saying 'order', losing the reminder aspect of the sentence. Option (d) unnecessarily complicates the sentence with 'should not', when the simple infinitive pattern ('not to forget') is the standard, natural way to report negative commands.

t: Mudassir warned the child, "Be careful and be slow."
o: ...that he be careful and be slow.
...to be careful and to be slow.
...to be careful and should be slow.
...that he should be careful and be slow.
e: When two commands are joined in one imperative sentence ('Be careful and be slow'), each command must be converted using its own 'to' plus base verb in indirect speech, keeping parallel structure: 'to be careful and to be slow'. Repeating 'to' before the second verb, rather than dropping it, is essential for grammatical parallelism. Option (a) does not use the infinitive form at all and awkwardly repeats 'that he be'. Option (c) mixes two different structures — 'to be careful' (infinitive) and 'should be slow' (modal) — breaking the required parallelism. Option (d) similarly mixes 'that he should' with a bare 'be slow', another parallel-structure violation.

t: Mr. Collin said, "Let me deliver the letters to the postman."
o: Mr. Collin said that let he be allowed to deliver the letters to the postman.
Mr. Collin requested that he might be allowed to deliver the letters to the postman.
Mr. Collin suggested with joy that he wished to deliver the letters to the postman.
Mr. Collin asked if he was allowed to deliver the letters to the postman.
e: 'Let me...' (the speaker asking permission for themselves) is different from 'Let him...' (permission for a third person) — it is converted using the pattern: 'requested that + subject + might be allowed to + verb'. Here the reporting verb becomes 'requested' (since the speaker is asking for permission for himself), the pronoun 'me' becomes 'he' (Mr. Collin, now spoken about in third person), and 'might' — not 'should' — is used, since this expresses possibility/permission rather than an order. Option (a) incorrectly keeps 'let' inside the 'that'-clause, which is ungrammatical. Option (c) invents a meaning ('wished to') not present in the original. Option (d) turns it into a question ('asked if'), when the original was a self-permission request, not a question directed at someone else.

t: Rita said, "Alas! I am ruined."
o: Rita said she was ruined.
Rita exclaimed with sorrow that she was ruined.
Rita said that she ruined.
Rita exclaimed sadly that I am ruined.
e: Exclamatory sentences (marked by interjections like 'Alas!', 'Hurrah!', 'Oh!') follow a special conversion pattern: the interjection is removed, the reporting verb becomes 'exclaimed with [emotion]' (matching the feeling the interjection conveys — here 'Alas!' signals sorrow), and the rest of the sentence becomes a normal statement with the usual tense-backshift and pronoun changes ('am' to 'was', 'I' to 'she'). Option (a) uses plain 'said' instead of the emotion-specific 'exclaimed with sorrow', losing the exclamatory tone. Option (c) incorrectly drops the verb 'ruined'. Option (d) correctly identifies the emotion but fails to change the pronoun and tense.

t: My little sister said, "What a beautiful sight!"
o: My little sister exclaimed that it was a beautiful sight.
My little sister said that it is a beautiful sight.
My little sister said that it had been a beautiful sight.
My little sister said that it would be a beautiful sight.
e: 'What a + adjective + noun!' is a standard exclamatory pattern showing admiration. In indirect speech it converts to: 'exclaimed that it was + adjective + noun', removing the 'What a...!' structure and replacing 'said' with the exclamation-specific 'exclaimed', along with a normal tense backshift of the implied 'is' to 'was'. Options (b), (c) and (d) all fail to use 'exclaimed' (keeping plain 'said'), missing the exclamatory tone entirely, and each applies the wrong tense — option (b) does not backshift at all, option (c) over-backshifts to Past Perfect, and option (d) wrongly turns it into a future statement.

t: "Oh, how could I ever thank you, Sir!" said the convict to the Bishop.
o: The convict exclaimed gratefully to the Bishop that how he could ever thank him.
The convict said to the Bishop that he could never thank him enough.
Exclaiming gratefully, the convict said to the Bishop that he could never thank him enough.
The convict told the Bishop that it was difficult for him to thank him.
e: This is a more advanced exclamatory pattern where 'How could I ever...!' (a rhetorical exclamation of overwhelming gratitude, not a literal question) is best expressed using a participle phrase, 'Exclaiming gratefully', at the start, combined with a rewritten statement capturing the same meaning: 'he could never thank him enough' — an idiomatic way of expressing extreme gratitude. This shows that Narration sometimes requires natural rewording rather than a mechanical word-for-word conversion. Option (a) keeps 'how' awkwardly inside the reported clause, mixing question and statement structure. Option (b) captures the right meaning but is missing the 'Exclaiming gratefully' element reflecting the emotion of 'Oh,...!'. Option (d) shifts the meaning to 'difficulty' rather than 'gratitude', missing the actual sense of the exclamation.

t: She said, "How beautiful is the rain!"
o: exclaimed with joy that the rain had been beautiful.
exclaimed with joy that the rain has been beautiful.
exclaimed with joy that the rain is beautiful.
exclaimed with joy that the rain was beautiful.
e: 'How + adjective + is/are + subject!' is another common exclamatory pattern expressing wonder about a quality, and it converts to: 'exclaimed with joy that + subject + was + adjective', with the 'How...!' structure removed and the reporting verb correctly changed from 'said' to 'exclaimed with joy'. The Present Tense 'is' backshifts normally to 'was', just like in any ordinary statement — exclamatory sentences follow the normal tense-backshift rules for their underlying verb, in addition to needing the emotional reporting verb and restructuring. Option (a) over-backshifts to Past Perfect, which is not needed here. Options (b) and (c) both fail to backshift the tense at all, keeping 'is' instead of 'was'.

t: He exclaimed that he was a very stupid fellow. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "How a stupid fellow are you!"
"What a stupid fellow you are!"
"Are you a stupid fellow!"
"How a stupid fellow you are!"
e: This reverse question tests the correct grammatical construction of an exclamatory sentence containing a noun ('fellow'). When exclaiming about a noun, English always uses 'What a + adjective + noun + subject + verb!' — never 'How a...!'. 'How' is reserved for exclaiming about adjectives or adverbs alone, without a following noun (e.g. 'How beautiful!', 'How fast he runs!'), while 'What' is used whenever a noun follows the adjective (e.g. 'What a beautiful house!'). Since 'fellow' is a noun here, only 'What a stupid fellow you are!' is grammatically correct. Options (a) and (d) both incorrectly use 'How' with a following noun, a very commonly tested error. Option (c) drops the exclamatory structure entirely and turns it into a plain question.

t: He observed that, had market liquidity vanished entirely, the exchange would have suspended trading. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "If market liquidity vanishes entirely, the exchange suspends trading."
"Had market liquidity vanished entirely, the exchange would have suspended trading."
"The exchange will suspend trading if market liquidity had vanished entirely."
"If the exchange suspended trading, it was because market liquidity vanished entirely."
e: This reinforces the same Third Conditional rule seen in the previous question: the complete 'Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle' structure must be reproduced exactly, without altering any of its internal tenses, since it already expresses a complete hypothetical past scenario (something that did not actually happen). Option (a) mistakenly converts it into a First Conditional (Present Simple plus Present Simple), changing the meaning from 'an unreal past possibility' to 'a real, general possibility' — a completely different type of conditional. Option (c) awkwardly mixes future tense with past perfect in a nonsensical combination. Option (d) restructures the sentence into a cause-and-effect explanation rather than preserving the original Third Conditional form.

t: She noted that, had the literary trope not been overused, the metaphor might still have resonated with the audience. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "If the literary trope was not overused, the metaphor may still resonate with the audience."
"Had the literary trope not been overused, the metaphor might still have resonated with the audience."
"Had the literary trope not been overused, the metaphor must still resonate with the audience."
"If the literary trope had not been overused, the metaphor will still resonate with the audience."
e: Building on the previous two questions, this additionally tests that the specific modal used inside a Third Conditional ('might have' here, expressing a weaker, more tentative possibility than 'would have') must also remain unchanged during conversion. 'Might have resonated' cannot be swapped for a different modal like 'must' (implying certainty, a completely different meaning) or 'may' (a present-tense modal, inconsistent with the past hypothetical structure). Option (a) both weakens the conditional type and changes 'might have' to 'may'. Option (c) wrongly substitutes 'must' for 'might', turning uncertainty into near-certainty. Option (d) mismatches a correct Third Conditional if-clause with a First-Conditional-style result clause, an inconsistent hybrid.

t: He asserted that the cryptographic protocol might have resisted the attack had entropy been truly random. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "Had entropy been truly random, the cryptographic protocol might have resisted the attack."
"If entropy is truly random, protocol might resist attack."
"If entropy had been random, protocol might resist attack."
"Entropy random, protocol resists attack."
e: This question shows that the two clauses of a conditional sentence can appear in either order (the 'had'-clause first, or the main result-clause first) without affecting the meaning or tense structure, as long as the internal tenses within each clause stay exactly as in the Third Conditional pattern. The correct answer simply reorders the clauses while preserving every tense correctly. Options (b) and (c) both incorrectly simplify the tense structure instead of using the full Third Conditional form. Option (d) drops essential grammar entirely, becoming an incomplete fragment rather than a properly formed sentence.

t: He confessed that the violin concerto would have remained fragmentary had the late maestro not bequeathed his annotated sketches. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The violin concerto would have remained fragmentary had the late maestro not bequeathed his annotated sketches."
"...if the late maestro not bequeathed his annotated sketches."
"...will be remaining fragmentary had the late maestro not bequeathed..."
"...would be fragmentary if sketches had not been bequeathed."
e: This final conditional question in the set confirms that the exact wording of a correctly-formed Third Conditional sentence — 'would have + past participle...had + subject + not + past participle' — must be reproduced precisely in Direct Speech, without alteration. Option (b) is grammatically broken, dropping the essential auxiliary 'had' from 'if the late maestro not bequeathed', which cannot form a valid conditional clause on its own (it needs either 'had...not bequeathed' or 'did not bequeath'). Option (c) wrongly uses the Present Continuous 'will be remaining' instead of 'would have remained', breaking the Third Conditional pattern entirely. Option (d) changes both the modal strength and the conditional clause structure, producing a weaker, inconsistent conditional type.

t: The zoologist warned that the island's carrying capacity might be exceeded should invasive species proliferate unchecked. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The island's carrying capacity will be exceeded if invasive species proliferate unchecked."
"Should invasive species have proliferated unchecked, the island's carrying capacity would be exceeded."
"The island's carrying capacity might be exceeded should invasive species proliferate unchecked."
"If invasive species proliferated unchecked, the carrying capacity had been exceeded."
e: 'Should + subject + base verb' (as in 'should invasive species proliferate') is an inverted, more formal way of writing an if-clause — it means exactly the same as 'if invasive species proliferate', just without the word 'if', with 'should' placed at the front and the subject and verb inverted. This inverted structure is a fixed alternative form and must be reproduced exactly, not rewritten using 'if'. Option (a) incorrectly converts it into an 'if'-clause and also wrongly strengthens the modal 'might' to 'will', changing the degree of certainty. Option (b) incorrectly adds 'have' ('should...have proliferated'), turning it into a Third Conditional past-hypothetical structure, when the original describes a general future possibility. Option (d) both converts to 'if' unnecessarily and produces a mismatched tense combination.

t: She indicated that, unless the quorum were met promptly, the charter amendments would lapse. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "Unless the quorum had been met promptly, the charter amendments would have lapsed."
"Unless the quorum is met promptly, the charter amendments will lapse."
"If the quorum was not met promptly, the charter amendments might have lapsed."
"If the quorum is promptly met, the charter amendments must not lapse."
e: This tests an important special case: when a conditional sentence expresses a general policy, rule, or standing procedure (rather than a one-time hypothetical event), it is treated similarly to a Universal Truth and uses the Present Tense in its Direct form, even though the indirect version uses a past-style subjunctive ('were met', 'would lapse'). The correct answer restores the Present and Future structure appropriate for a standing organizational rule: 'unless the quorum is met...the amendments will lapse'. Option (a) wrongly turns it into a Third Conditional (past-hypothetical) structure, which does not fit a general, recurring rule. Option (c) unnecessarily replaces 'unless' with 'if...not' and weakens the certainty with 'might have lapsed'. Option (d) changes the meaning entirely by adding an obligation ('must not lapse') not present in the original.

t: The lecturer argued that, given sufficient entropic isolation, the reaction rate could asymptotically approach zero. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "Given sufficient entropic isolation, the reaction rate could asymptotically approach zero."
"If sufficient entropic isolation was given, the reaction rate will asymptotically approach zero."
"Given sufficient entropic isolation, the reaction rate can asymptotically approach zero."
"If the reaction rate approached zero, it must have had sufficient entropic isolation."
e: This question checks whether students can distinguish 'could' (used here for a real, present-tense theoretical possibility, similar to but slightly softer than 'can', common in academic writing) from 'can' — since the indirect sentence already uses 'could', not 'can', the Direct Speech version must keep 'could' exactly as it is. Also, 'given sufficient entropic isolation' (meaning 'if there is/were sufficient entropic isolation') is fixed academic phrasing that should not be converted into an 'if'-clause. Option (b) incorrectly turns this into a mismatched 'if'-clause. Option (c) wrongly swaps 'could' for 'can', changing the intended nuance. Option (d) drastically restructures the sentence into a reversed cause-effect statement that does not match the original meaning.

t: The ethicist argued that, absent informed consent, the study's methodology was fundamentally untenable. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "Absent informed consent, the study's methodology is fundamentally untenable."
"If the study lacked informed consent, its methodology had been fundamentally untenable."
"Without informed consent, the study's methodology would have been fundamentally untenable."
"The study's methodology must have been untenable since it lacked informed consent."
e: 'Absent X' is a formal academic phrase meaning 'without X' or 'in the absence of X', and when used to state a general principle (as here — an ethical/methodological principle about research, not a one-time event), the sentence is treated like a Universal Truth and its Present Tense is restored in Direct Speech, even though the indirect version shows 'was' due to the normal backshift from a past reporting verb. Option (b) wrongly restructures the phrase into an 'if'-clause and creates a mismatched, ungrammatical tense combination. Option (c) turns the general principle into a Third-Conditional-like hypothetical ('would have been'), removing its 'general truth' quality. Option (d) restructures the sentence into a different logical form (a deduction, 'must have been'), changing what kind of statement this originally was.

t: The envoy reported that the negotiations were languishing because neither party would concede procedural precedence. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The negotiations languish because neither party would concede procedural precedence."
"The negotiations are languishing because neither party will be conceding procedural precedence."
"The negotiations are languishing because neither party will concede procedural precedence."
"Negotiations languished, no party conceding precedence."
e: This reverse question requires two separate corrections: Past Continuous 'were languishing' reverses to Present Continuous 'are languishing' (describing an ongoing, current situation at the time of the original statement), and the modal 'would' reverses to 'will' (Simple Future, not continuous). Option (a) fails to reverse the continuous tense at all, keeping bare Simple Present 'languish'. Option (b) incorrectly uses 'will be conceding' (Future Continuous), when the correct reversal of 'would concede' (Simple Conditional) is simply 'will concede' (Simple Future) — no continuous aspect was originally present. Option (d) drops proper sentence structure and tense entirely, becoming an incomplete, non-standard fragment.

t: The curator noted that the pigments were deteriorating faster than the varnish could protect them. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The pigments are deteriorating faster than the varnish can protect them."
"The pigments were deteriorating faster than the varnish can be protected by them."
"Pigments deteriorate faster than varnish protects."
"Pigment deterioration faster than varnish can protect."
e: Similar to the previous question, this reverses two elements together: Past Continuous 'were deteriorating' reverses to Present Continuous 'are deteriorating' (an ongoing observed process), and the modal 'could' reverses to 'can' (Simple Present ability or possibility). Option (b) confusingly switches to passive voice ('can be protected by them'), reversing the roles of subject and object and changing the meaning — it should stay active, 'the varnish can protect them', not passive. Option (c) drops the continuous aspect and the modal entirely, oversimplifying into a generic present statement that does not match the original observation. Option (d) is grammatically broken, missing a proper verb and complete sentence structure.

t: The botanist sighed that the rare orchid had germinated, only to succumb to a latent fungal blight. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The rare orchid did germinate, only to succumb to a latent fungal blight."
"A rare orchid had germinated only to succumb to a latent fungal blight."
"The rare orchid germinated, only to succumb to a latent fungal blight."
"Rare orchid germinates but succumbs to fungus."
e: This reverses Past Perfect back to Simple Past: 'had germinated' reverses to plain 'germinated', since Past Perfect in Indirect Speech (used because the reporting verb 'sighed' is past) simply reflects the ordinary Simple Past of the original quoted sentence. Option (a) incorrectly uses the emphatic 'did germinate' construction, which would only be used for special emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'It DID germinate, despite the odds') — not the neutral, default reversal needed here. Option (b) wrongly changes 'the rare orchid' (a specific orchid already known) to 'a rare orchid' (introducing it as new/unspecified), altering the article and the implied context. Option (d) uses Present Tense throughout, losing the past, completed nature of the event the botanist was describing.

t: The historian observed that the records had been tampered with. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "Someone tampered with the records."
"The records had been tampered with."
"The records are tampered with."
"The records are fake."
e: This question demonstrates an important exception: Past Perfect is not always reversed to a simpler tense in Direct Speech — sometimes the original quoted sentence was already in Past Perfect, especially when the action being described happened clearly before another past reference point. In such cases, Direct Speech retains 'had been tampered with' exactly as it appears in the Indirect version, rather than automatically simplifying it. Option (a) completely changes the sentence structure from passive to active, changing the meaning. Option (c) wrongly shifts to Present Tense, losing the past context entirely. Option (d) rewrites the meaning altogether — 'are fake' is not equivalent to 'had been tampered with'.

t: He commented that the policy's efficacy would remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrued. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The efficacy of the policy remains conjectural as the data are yet to be collected."
"The policy's efficacy will remain conjectural until longitudinal data accrue."
"Until longitudinal data had accrued, the policy's efficacy might have remained conjectural."
"Efficacy remains conjecture till data accumulates."
e: This tests two combined rules: 'would' reverses to 'will' (Simple Future), and the verb inside a time-clause introduced by 'until' ('accrued', functioning here as a subjunctive, timeless form typical of formal future time-clauses) reverses to its base/present form 'accrue'. This reflects the general English rule that future time-clauses beginning with words like 'until', 'when', 'before', 'after', and 'as soon as' never use 'will' or a future form inside them — they use a present-tense verb even though the overall sentence refers to future time. Option (a) is a paraphrase that loses the 'will remain...until' future time-clause pattern. Option (c) incorrectly treats this as a past-hypothetical, Third-Conditional-like sentence, which does not match the original future-oriented meaning. Option (d) is an oversimplified paraphrase that changes the wording and structure significantly.

t: The mentor noted that the fellow had persevered even after his hypotheses were repeatedly falsified. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "The fellow persevered even after your hypotheses were repeatedly falsified."
"The fellow persevered even after his hypotheses were repeatedly falsified."
"The fellow preserve though hypotheses are falsified."
"The fellow had persevered though his hypotheses were repeatedly falsified."
e: Here, 'had persevered' reverses to Simple Past 'persevered', because both actions in the sentence (persevering, and the hypotheses being falsified) occurred within the same general past timeframe as part of a connected narrative, without one clearly happening much earlier than the other — so no extra Past Perfect layer is needed in the direct quote. The pronoun 'his' stays 'his' in both versions since the mentor is speaking about a third person (the fellow) throughout, with no shift in perspective involved. Option (a) incorrectly changes 'his' to 'your', which would only be correct if the mentor were speaking directly to the fellow, but the context shows he is describing the fellow to someone else. Option (c) breaks basic subject-verb agreement and inconsistently mixes tenses. Option (d) unnecessarily keeps 'had persevered' in Past Perfect, which is not needed once reversed to Direct Speech.

t: The patient said, "It has been three days since I last slept."
o: The patient said that it was three days since he last slept.
The patient said that it had been three days since he had last slept.
The patient said that he didn't sleep for three days.
The patient said that he was not sleeping for three days.
e: This sentence requires backshifting in two separate places within the same clause: the main verb 'has been' (Present Perfect) backshifts to 'had been' (Past Perfect), and the verb inside the 'since'-clause, 'last slept' (Simple Past), also backshifts further to 'had last slept' (Past Perfect) — both parts must shift together, since both were originally anchored to the present moment of speaking. Option (a) only backshifts the first verb and misses backshifting the second verb inside the since-clause. Options (c) and (d) both abandon the original since-clause structure and reword the meaning, losing the precise 'three days since...' time relationship the original sentence expresses.

t: "I've just bought a car," said Amar, "But it isn't insured yet. So I cannot take you for a ride."
o: ...he just bought a car but it wasn't insured till then. So, he could not take me for a ride.
...he had just bought a car but it wasn't insured till then. So, he could not be taken for a ride.
...he had just bought the car but it wasn't insured till then. So, he could not take me for a ride.
...he had just bought a car but it wasn't insured till then. So, he could not take me for a ride.
e: This multi-sentence quote requires several coordinated changes applied consistently: 'have just bought' (Present Perfect) backshifts to 'had just bought' (Past Perfect); 'isn't' (Simple Present negative) backshifts to 'wasn't' (Simple Past negative); 'yet' changes to 'till then'; and 'cannot' backshifts to 'could not'. Importantly, the article stays 'a car', not 'the car' — because 'a car' was how it was first introduced (as something new/unspecified), and this should not change just because we are reporting it later, since that would wrongly imply the listener already knew which specific car was meant. Option (a) fails to backshift 'just bought' to Past Perfect. Option (b) wrongly turns 'take me' (active) into a passive 'be taken', changing who performs the action. Option (c) makes the same article mistake, using 'the car' instead of 'a car'.

t: Hari said to the boy, "What's the matter? Why are you crying? Be cheerful."
o: Hari asked the boy what the matter was and why he was crying. He asked him to be cheerful.
Hari asks the boy what the matter was and why he was crying. He asks him to be cheerful.
Hari asked the boy what the matter was and why he was crying. He asks him to be cheerful.
Hari asked the boy what was the matter and he was crying. He asked him to be cheerful.
e: This sentence combines three different sentence types in one quote — two Wh-questions ('What's the matter?', 'Why are you crying?') and one Imperative ('Be cheerful') — and each must be converted according to its own rule, while keeping the reporting verbs consistently in the past tense throughout. The two Wh-questions use 'asked' plus normal statement word order: 'what the matter was' and 'why he was crying'. The imperative 'Be cheerful' converts to 'asked him to be cheerful' (object plus to plus base verb). Options (b) and (c) incorrectly switch to present-tense reporting verbs partway through, creating an inconsistent tense within a single passage — once you start reporting in the past, you must stay consistent throughout. Option (d) wrongly keeps the inverted question word order 'what was the matter'.

t: The teacher paused and said, "Those who are tired of listening to me can go. I shall not mind it."
o: ...ordered that those who were tired of listening to him would go and that he would not mind that.
...paused and then said that those who have been tired of listening to him would go...

e: This sentence contains two separate but related statements that must be combined smoothly into one connected Indirect Speech sentence, joined using 'that' as a connector: 'are tired' backshifts to 'were tired', the modal 'can' backshifts to 'could' (permission being reported, not obligation), and 'I shall not mind' backshifts to 'he would not mind' with the correct first-to-third-person pronoun change. Option (a) incorrectly uses 'ordered' as the reporting verb, when the original tone is permissive rather than a command, and it wrongly backshifts 'can' all the way to 'would' instead of 'could'. Option (b) fails to backshift the tense correctly and does not backshift 'can' to 'could' at all. Option (c) fails to backshift any of the tenses or pronouns, essentially leaving the sentence almost unchanged, which is incorrect since a past reporting verb requires backshifting.

t: He ordered his soldiers to take that bird away. Its gilded cage reminded him of his father whom he had imprisoned. (Convert to DIRECT)
o: "May this bird be taken away. Its gilded cage reminds me of my father whom I imprisoned."
"Take the bird away. Its gilded cage reminded him of his father whom I imprison."
"Take this bird away. Its gilded cage reminded me of my father whom I imprison."
"Take this bird away. Its gilded cage reminds me of my father whom I imprisoned."
e: This reverse question requires careful, separate treatment of each part of the sentence. The imperative 'ordered...to take' reverses to a plain command, 'Take', with no auxiliary needed. 'That bird' (distant, as referred to by the reporter) reverses to 'this bird' (near, as the speaker himself would refer to it while looking at it directly). 'Reminded' (Simple Past, describing his ongoing feeling as reported in the past) reverses to 'reminds' (Present Tense), reflecting a present, ongoing emotional reaction at the moment of speaking rather than a one-time past event. Finally, 'had imprisoned' (Past Perfect, describing a single, clearly-completed past action before the 'reminding' moment) stays as 'imprisoned' (Simple Past) since it refers to a genuinely completed past event needing no further reversal. Options (a) and (c) incorrectly use present-tense 'imprison' for a clearly completed past action. Option (b) wrongly leaves 'reminded' unreversed and uses 'him' instead of the correct first-person 'me'.

t: "Dear daughter," she said caressing her cheeks, "have you come to comfort me in my time of need?"
o: Caressing her daughter's cheeks, she asked affectionately if she had come to comfort her in her time of need.
...she said affectionately if she had been coming to comfort her in her time of need.
...she asked affectionately if she did come to comfort her in her time of need.
...she said affectionately if she has come to comfort her in her time of need.
e: This sentence tests several advanced points together: the direct address 'Dear daughter' is simply deleted in Indirect Speech (terms of address are not reported literally), while the participle phrase 'Caressing her cheeks' (describing an action happening alongside the speech) is retained and simply repositioned, with 'her' now clearly referring back to 'her daughter's cheeks'. Since the direct sentence is a Yes/No question, the reporting verb correctly becomes 'asked' (not 'said') — and since it carries a warm, loving tone, 'affectionately' reflects that. Finally, Present Perfect 'have you come' backshifts to Past Perfect 'had she come', with normal statement word order (no inversion). Option (b) incorrectly uses 'said' instead of 'asked' and wrongly changes the tense to Past Perfect Continuous. Option (c) also wrongly uses 'said' and incorrectly inserts 'did come' instead of the correct Past Perfect. Option (d) uses 'said' instead of 'asked' and fails to backshift the tense at all.

t: You said, "Priya kept watching television till her mother exploded at her."
o: You said that Priya had kept watching television till her mother exploded at her.
You said that Priya kept watching television till her mother had exploded at her.
You said that Priya kept watching television till her mother exploded at her.
You said that Priya had kept watching television till her mother had exploded at her.
e: This question demonstrates an important exception to the normal backshift rule: when the direct speech quote is itself already a complete, self-contained narrative describing a sequence of past events (here, connected by 'till', showing one action continuing until another happened), and both actions are already clearly in Simple Past showing their own internal sequence, no further backshift into Past Perfect is applied — the Simple Past tenses are left exactly as they are, because backshifting them further would distort the clear 'till' sequence relationship between the two actions. Options (a), (b) and (d) all incorrectly add extra Past Perfect backshifting to one or both verbs, which is unnecessary and would confuse the timeline, since the sentence already tells a complete past story with its own internal sequencing via 'till'.

e: This challenging reverse question requires three coordinated reversals: the pronoun 'they' (referring to Isha and Shivani together, as seen by an outside reporter) reverses to 'we' (since Isha is now speaking about herself and Shivani together, in her own direct words); 'didn't need' (Simple Past negative) reverses to 'don't need' (Simple Present negative); and 'had been given' (Past Perfect Passive) reverses to 'have been given' (Present Perfect Passive). Option (a) correctly reverses the pronoun and negative tense but incorrectly uses 'am given' (Simple Present Passive) instead of 'have been given' (Present Perfect Passive). Options (c) and (d) incorrectly keep 'they' instead of changing it to 'we', which would only be correct if someone other than Isha herself were speaking these words directly.

t: Mahendra told her that he would be waiting for her at the theatre. (Convert to DIRECT)

e: This reverse question requires three coordinated reversals happening together: 'would' (backshifted future) reverses to 'will' (Simple Future); 'he' (third person, as spoken about by someone reporting Mahendra's words) reverses to 'I' (since Mahendra is now speaking his own words in Direct Speech); and 'her' (referring to the listener, from an outside reporter's perspective) reverses to 'you' (since Mahendra is now speaking directly to her). The reporting verb correctly stays as 'told' (not 'asked'), since the original sentence is a plain statement, not a question. Option (a) fails to reverse the pronouns. Options (b) and (c) incorrectly change the reporting verb to 'asked'/'inquired', which are only appropriate for questions, not statements.

Alongside this, 'would' reverses to 'will' as usual. Option (a) fails to reverse 'would' to 'will', leaving it in the backshifted form. Option (b) both fails to reverse the modal properly (introducing the unrelated 'have to') and misses updating 'then' appropriately. Option (d) correctly reverses 'would' to 'will' but wrongly keeps 'then' instead of the correct 'now' — remembering that time-and-place words reverse just as tenses do is essential in these reverse-conversion questions.

t: Iba said that she might go home the next day with her sister.

t: He said that he intended to leave for Surat that night.

"I intend to leave for Surat tonight" he said.

e: Ek khaas Exception (Apwaad) yaad rakhna: Jab kisi Time Clause (jo 'when' ya 'while' se shuru ho) mein Past Tense hota hai aur sath mein dusra past action hota hai, toh indirect banate waqt Tense change nahi kiya jata. Isliye "was a child" aur "wasn't afraid" as it is rahenge, bas pronoun 'I' ka 'he' banega.

t:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in reported speech.
Raghav said to Meera, "Are you upset with me?"
o: Raghav asked Meera if she was upset with her.
Raghav asked Meera if she was upset with him.
Raghav asked Meera if she was upset with me.
Raghav asked Meera why she was upset with him.
e:
In the case of Interrogative sentences like this, "said" in Direct Speech is changed into "enquired (of)", "wanted to know", "asked", etc.
In Indirect speech, the verb is always placed after the subject, unlike in Direct Speech.
If there is a question in the Direct Speech whose answer can come as "Yes" or "No" in the Indirect Speech, we should use the conjunctions "if" or "whether".
For example:
Ravi said to me, "Is she studying?" (Direct Speech)
Ravi asked me if she was studying. (Indirect Speech)
Also, the sentence in the Direct Speech is in the Simple Present tense. So, the tense in the Indirect Speech should be in the Simple Past tense.
The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:
'If' would be introduced in the sentence.
The pronouns 'you' and 'me' would be changed to 'she' and 'him' respectively.
'Are you' would be changed to 'she was'.
Therefore, the correct answer is option (b): Raghav asked Meera if she was upset with him.

e:
In the case of Interrogative sentences like this, "enquired (of)", "wanted to know", "asked", etc in Indirect Speech is changed into "said" in Direct Speech.
In Direct speech, the verb is always placed before the subject, unlike in Indirect Speech.
For example:
The teacher asked him what his name was. (Indirect Speech)
The teacher said to him, "What is your name?" (Direct Speech)
The tense of the Indirect Speech is in the past continuous. So, the tense in the Direct Speech will be in the present continuous.
The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:
· 'was doing' changes to 'are doing'.
· 'I' changes to 'you'.
· 'my' changes to 'your'.
Therefore, the correct answer is: Hira said to me, "How are you doing being all alone in your house?"
